newsitem.title: INDIA: Cotton - India moving towards revival of futures.
newsitem.headline: Cotton - India moving towards revival of futures.

text.p: India is moving towards a revival of futures trading in cotton after a gap of nearly three decades, traders said on Thursday.
"We have to strengthen the existing infrastructure. Some fine-tuning is required and that is being done," said C.H. Mirani, former president of the East India Cotton Association (EICA).
He said consent for starting futures trading had been given by both the finance and textile ministries. "It is round the corner...not later than two months."
India banned futures trading in cotton in 1966 in a bid to prevent speculation and hoarding and to stabilise prices.
Mirani said that the infrastructure to carry out forward trade was already available through the currently functioning Cotton Exchange which now oversees spot delivery deals.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, in the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April/March) announced that the government had decided to allow cotton futures trading, a long-standing EICA demand.
"We have to ensure transparency in futures trade dealings. So the system that we need to follow should be most modern," Mirani said.
EICA had urged the revival of futures trading in cotton after India initiated economic reforms in 1991.
It said India had now emerged as a surplus cotton producer and that restrictions on trade needed to be removed.

"Futures trading will, apart from checking steep falls and sharp rises in prices, serve as a hedging tool to various functionaries such as merchants, mills, exporters and provide price guidance to them," said EICA president Suresh Kotak.
"It will benefit cotton growers by ensuring better prices and help the cotton economy in the long run," he said.
India's cotton crop in the 1996/97 (October/September) season has been officially estimated at 16 million bales (one bale is 170 kg), the same as in the previous year.
The government has so far allowed exports of 1.2 million bales in the current season against 1.59 bales in 1995/96.
In the week to Thursday, cotton prices remained firm, despite losing part of the initial gains, on hopes the government would allow more exports in the current season.
The announcement did not come through but reduced crop arrivals helped prices recover and stay firm during the week.
In spot, Bengal-deshi rose 45/50 rupees to 885/950 rupees per maund (37.32 kgs). Punjab saw-ginned gained 30 rupees to 1,490/1,630 rupees per maund.
Gujarat Kalyan (medium-staple) firmed 500/800 rupees to 12,000/12,500 rupees per candy (355.56 kg).
Traders said about 12-13 million bales of the new crop had been marketed so far.
"I am expecting limited arrivals and there could be a shortage of good quality cotton in the coming days," said a trader.
-- Bombay Commodities +91-22-265 9000
